items.abstract: WHEN A CIVILIZATION NO LONGER KNOWS WHERE TO PLACE ITS PEOPLE A BIT Essay on Education, Work, Human Value, and the Finite Human Life Cycle Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This interdisciplinary social and philosophical essay examines a growing concern in modern civilization: the potential disconnection between human educational achievement, accumulated capabilities, labor-market structures, and meaningful participation in society. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay begins with a reported case of a highly educated individual experiencing prolonged difficulty entering stable employment. Rather than interpreting an individual case as evidence of universal labor-market failure, the essay investigates the structural interfaces between education, professional training, recruitment, technological change, and the finite human life cycle. A central argument is that education, businesses, technological systems, and public institutions often operate on different timescales. Education may require many years. Recruitment decisions may be made within months. Technologies can transform occupations rapidly, while human lives continue through irreversible biological and social stages. When these systems become misaligned, the costs of institutional mismatch may be transferred disproportionately to individuals. The essay introduces a BIT interpretation of historical outcomes (Quả lịch sử), emphasizing that a person's abilities and achievements represent accumulated life histories rather than isolated qualifications or current employment status. It discusses the compression of human capabilities into résumés, the disappearance of entry-level opportunities, unused professional knowledge, and the potential loss of social participation when qualified individuals cannot find meaningful opportunities to contribute. The essay proposes examining the transition between education and employment as an important form of social infrastructure. Possible responses include professional transition pathways, mentorship, supervised work opportunities, recognition of transferable capabilities, and institutions capable of connecting human knowledge with real societal needs. Central Proposition A civilization should not be evaluated only by how many people it educates, but also by its ability to transform their accumulated knowledge and capabilities into meaningful participation in collective life. Scope and Limitations This publication is a social and philosophical thought essay, not an empirical demonstration that higher education has lost its value or that artificial intelligence is the cause of unemployment. It does not treat a single reported employment case as representative of the entire labor market. Its purpose is to encourage interdisciplinary discussion about education, employment, human dignity, institutional responsibility, and the preservation of human potential throughout finite life cycles. The original Vietnamese essay references reporting from The Wall Street Journal and materials from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the National Science Foundation's National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. items.abstract: When the Collective Foundation Changes Rhythm A Conditional Foresight Essay on Children, Digital Environments, and the New Historical Outcomes of Humanity Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This conditional foresight essay explores how changes in modern environments may influence the formation, transmission, and transformation of collective behavioral foundations across generations. Developed from Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Source Ontology Framework 03, the essay examines the relationship between intrinsic human characteristics, historical collective foundations, environmental change, and emerging technological systems. The central question concerns what may happen when the environments shaping human development change much faster than the biological and structural characteristics of human beings. The essay explores nine conditional future perspectives, including: The increasing difference between long-term intrinsic human characteristics and rapidly changing environments. Digital screens and online interactions becoming major channels through which children acquire and retain experiences. Changes in the relative influence of families, schools, digital platforms, and artificial intelligence on childhood development. Individuals participating simultaneously in multiple overlapping historical and cultural collective foundations. Artificial intelligence becoming an active component in cycles of information retention, behavioral feedback, and social interaction. The growing difficulty of separating intrinsic tendencies from environmentally acquired behavior. Educational approaches moving beyond immediate measurable outcomes toward the design of developmental environments. Societies recognizing how their institutions, technologies, and daily practices shape the foundations inherited by future generations. The possibility of multiple future developmental trajectories rather than one predetermined collective destiny. The BIT cycle Tính – Lưu – Hành – Quả – Tính serves as a conceptual framework for considering how environmental interactions become retained patterns and how present outcomes influence subsequent generations. A central idea is that every generation inherits not only an existing world but also historically established rhythms, practices, expectations, and systems of interaction. Through its activities, each generation may preserve, transform, or replace parts of these inherited foundations. The essay does not assume that digital technology is universally beneficial or harmful. Its potential effects depend on technological design, family environments, education, communities, institutions, and the specific histories of different societies. Scientific scope and limitations This publication is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or an experimentally validated theory of human development. It does not predict that collective human behavior must follow a single technological, social, or historical trajectory. The proposed perspectives are intended to encourage interdisciplinary discussion about childhood, education, technological environments, human adaptability, artificial intelligence, and responsibility toward future generations. items.abstract: WHEN A DEGREE IS NO LONGER A PROMISE A Conditional Foresight Essay on Education, Employment, and Human Life-Cycle Transition Infrastructure Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This conditional foresight essay explores possible transformations in education, employment, professional identity, and social institutions as artificial intelligence, automation, and rapidly changing economic structures reshape the relationship between human knowledge and work. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay asks whether future civilization will be able to maintain meaningful transitions between learning, professional contribution, personal development, and a dignified human life. The essay presents nine conditional future perspectives. First, academic degrees may increasingly function as evidence of educational achievement rather than implicit guarantees of specific professional positions. Second, automation and artificial intelligence may reduce certain entry-level tasks, potentially weakening traditional pathways through which younger generations acquire professional experience. Third, institutions may develop transferable capability profiles that recognize practical skills, interdisciplinary competence, and demonstrated problem-solving ability beyond conventional occupational titles. Fourth, universities may expand their responsibilities by supporting graduates through longer professional transitions rather than ending institutional support at graduation. Fifth, countries may begin treating unused human expertise as a potential public resource, creating mechanisms to connect available capabilities with unmet social needs. Sixth, careers may increasingly involve multiple transitions among employment, education, independent work, care responsibilities, and periods of recovery. Seventh, artificial intelligence may improve labor-market matching while simultaneously creating new risks of algorithmic exclusion, opacity, and unfair screening. Eighth, future institutions may recognize periods of unemployment, retraining, caregiving, and independent research as legitimate phases of human development rather than treating them as personal deficiencies. Ninth, the evaluation of education and employment policies may shift toward their long-term effects on the complete human life cycle, including health, family formation, professional resilience, social participation, and security in later life. Central Proposition The future value of education may depend not only on academic credentials, but also on whether civilization develops effective bridges between human learning, meaningful contribution, and dignified life transitions. The essay suggests that education, employers, governments, and technological systems may need to share responsibility for maintaining these pathways. Scope and Limitations This publication is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or an empirically established prediction. items.title: Knowing When to Hand Over: A Survey of Uncertainty, Deferral, and Escalation in Human–AI Fraud Investigation
items.abstract: Language-model agents are being proposed to investigate fraud and money-laundering alerts under selective autonomy: the agent closes some cases itself and escalates the rest to a human analyst. Which cases it escalates determines the division of labor, the analysts' workload, and the errors that reach customers and regulators, yet the knowledge needed to design that rule is divided among learning to defer and selective prediction, uncertainty estimation for language models, and research on human reliance on AI advice. This survey connects the three through the escalation loop of a fraud-investigation team and restates known results from these literatures in one notation. We state the cost-optimal escalation rule, which requires different confidence thresholds for closing a case as benign and for concluding fraud, and its form under a fixed analyst capacity; show that calibration suffices for selective risk to be monotone and interpretable; state the conformal bound on the rate of cases that are both closed automatically and wrong; show when combining uncertainty signals helps and when correlated signals double-count; show that the error among automatically closed cases is not identified without audits and is estimable with them; and quantify how analyst reliance on the agent's verdict erodes the value of escalation. Against this basis we compare deferral rules and uncertainty signals, and conclude that threshold-based deferral rules assume a calibrated confidence that agents do not yet provide, that agent-level uncertainty estimation is only beginning, and that, to our knowledge, no peer-reviewed study has yet evaluated an escalation rule for a fraud-investigation agent together with the analysts who receive its cases.

items.title: Knowledge as Code
items.abstract: For millennia, knowledge has been carried by language, and large language models still put language at the center. Yet the coding agents built on these models mostly write code. This paper is a contribution to epistemology, which asks what kind of knowledge code is and how it is obtained. We define knowledge as code as knowledge written in a programming language or in a machine-parsable data format, whose validity can be checked by executing it. We define thirteen epistemic properties of knowledge media and show that code is the first medium to have all of them. We distinguish two ways in which knowledge enters code, encoding and learning by execution, where code is both the experiment and the record of its result. Agents make learning by execution observable, since their trajectories record every probe, observation and line of code they keep. Code is thus not only a tool of knowledge work but a knowledge medium in its own right, the first that can check what it holds.

items.title: La inteligencia artificial y sus implicaciones antihumanistas. Consecuencias de la delegación de la responsabilidad del pensar en las máquinas
items.abstract: Various voices warn of the growing anti-humanism that prevails today. This risk of the devaluation of humanity finds a salient example—in the context of posthumanism in its cybernetic form—in the unstoppable development of AI with the emergence of products such as ChatGPT, capable of generating literary, musical, or pictorial compositions. This is a technology that enables humans to delegate to non-thinking machines the responsibility for the task of thinking in its different domains—cognitive, evaluative, or artistic creation— thus running the risk of falling back, in Kantian terms, into a condition of immaturity. The task of thought—and, therefore, of philosophy—should consist in remaining vigilant in order to resist such temptations and, if possible, in exercising with greater firmness that faculty of thinking characteristic of humans, by analyzing the age in which they find themselves and the dangers that lie in wait for them.

items.title: Labor markets and inequality
items.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) changes labor markets and the distribution of income. It begins by distinguishing skill-biased, routine-biased, and task-biased technological change, then explains why generative AI requires a further shift in emphasis from occupations to tasks, workflows, and organizational control. The chapter argues that AI affects inequality through several channels at once: direct task displacement, productivity gains, the creation of new tasks, changes in market power, and differences in worker bargaining power. A central claim is that exposure to AI is not the same as technological unemployment. The distributional consequences depend on adoption costs, complementary investments, institutions, and the allocation of productivity rents inside firms and across markets. This chapter, therefore, treats AI neither as an automatic engine of mass unemployment nor as a neutral productivity tool, but as a general-purpose technology whose labor market effects are mediated by economic structure and policy.

items.title: Language Impairment as a Lens onto Large Language Models
items.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.

items.title: Large Language Model-Tuned Rule Distillation for Adversarial Ramp Cut-in Testing of Autonomous Vehicles
items.abstract: Highway ramp merging is a safety-critical interaction for automated-vehicle validation because gap acceptance, longitudinal control, and lane-changing responses are coupled within a short time horizon. This paper presents a rule-distillation framework in which a large language model (LLM) serves only as an offline calibrator of a compact, interpretable rule expert: the model receives scalar replay statistics and proposes bounded updates of three rule parameters, every candidate is verified by closed-loop simulation, and the accepted rule expert is re-executed under legal-action masking and safety filtering to produce feasible demonstrations for an adversarial ramp actor, which is then fine-tuned by multi-agent reinforcement learning on a fixed scenario-replay library. On the training-distribution library, the distilled adversary reaches the highest evaluation return and reward-collision rate of the three schemes. This advantage only partly carries over to 150 held-out scenarios, where its reward-collision rate becomes indistinguishable from that of training from scratch (42.7% against 40.7%, overlapping intervals) while its evaluation return and its rate of successfully induced evasive responses remain higher. Against random-search and Bayesian-optimization calibrators evaluated under the same parameter ranges, score and simulation budget, the LLM attains a comparable calibration score with roughly one third of the closed-loop simulations and with a smaller run-to-run spread, but it is not a better global optimizer at the full budget, so it is best characterized as a sample-efficient and low-variance calibrator. The results indicate that verified rule calibration provides effective initialization for adversarial reinforcement learning within the evaluated simulation setting.

items.title: Latent profile analysis of AI anxiety among medical imaging students: a cross-sectional study based on emotional flexibility and future employment anxiety
items.abstract: Objective This study aimed to identify latent profiles of AI anxiety among medical imaging students and to examine the associations of emotional flexibility, future employment anxiety, and demographic variables with profile membership, thereby providing empirical evidence for differentiated psychological intervention strategies. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted using convenience sampling among 488 medical imaging students recruited from North Sichuan Medical College in Sichuan Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale, the Emotional Flexibility Scale, the Future Employment Anxiety Scale, and a demographic questionnaire. Latent profile analysis was used to identify AI anxiety profiles, and the three-step BCH and R3STEP procedures were used to examine distal outcomes and covariates while accounting for classification uncertainty. Results Latent profile analysis identified three severity-ordered AI anxiety profiles: a Medium AI anxiety profile (65.78%), a High AI anxiety profile (22.75%), and a Low AI anxiety profile (11.48%). The High profile scored most prominently on Job Replacement and Sociotechnical Blindness anxiety. Emotional flexibility showed a nonlinear distribution across profiles: highest in the Low profile (BCH M = 3.975), lowest in the Medium profile (3.282), and intermediate in the High profile (3.805). Future employment anxiety increased monotonically across the profiles (Low: 2.285; Medium: 3.255; High: 4.126; all pairwise p < 0.001) and independently distinguished all profiles in the classification-error-adjusted (R3STEP) analysis. Emotional flexibility was lowest in the Medium profile and did not differ between the High and Low profiles ( p = 0.271); in the classification-error-adjusted analysis, it distinguished the High from the Medium profile but not the Low from the Medium profile. Conclusion The findings support differentiated psychological support tailored to distinct AI anxiety profiles, and suggest that AI literacy education and career planning guidance should be systematically integrated into medical imaging curricula.

items.abstract: Leadership in Neurodiverse, AI-Augmented Organizations explores the evolving nature of leadership in an era where artificial intelligence and human diversity are reshaping the future of work. As organizations increasingly adopt AI-powered technologies and embrace inclusive workplace practices, leaders are challenged to cultivate environments that value diverse cognitive abilities, foster innovation, and ensure ethical, people-centered decision-making. This edited volume brings together scholarly research, conceptual insights, empirical studies, and practical case analyses that examine how leadership can successfully integrate AI capabilities while empowering neurodiverse talent. It highlights the importance of adaptive leadership, emotional intelligence, digital transformation, inclusive organizational cultures, and responsible AI governance in building resilient and high-performing organizations.

items.title: Learn to Modify: Self-evolving Multi-agent Refinement Framework for Conversational Text-to-Motion Generation
items.abstract: Despite rapid progress in text-to-motion generation, existing methods are commonly designed for single-shot generation. When users are dissatisfied with specific motion details, they are often forced to regenerate the entire sequence from scratch, which is computationally inefficient and potentially destroys previously established kinematic context. A practical generation system should instead support iterative user feedback and refine only the affected spatio-temporal regions while preserving the remaining motion. Therefore, we introduce a conversational motion generation paradigm that requires the system to coordinate instruction understanding, motion generation, localized editing, and quality assessment. Recent advances in LLM-driven multi-agent systems provide a promising foundation for such role-specialized coordination. To tackle these challenges, a Self-evolving Multi-Agent RefinemenT Framework (SMART) is proposed for conversational motion generation. Within SMART, to preserve semantic consistency, we design a semantic-guided masked motion editing mechanism, which precisely grounds natural language feedback into spatiotemporal motion regions to enable localized refinements without altering unedited regions. To reduce redundant exploration, we propose a memory-based self-evolving strategy that dynamically accumulates motion editing knowledge from interaction history and reuses past successful experience. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SMART effectively supports multi-turn conversational motion generation and enables efficient motion refinement.

items.title: Learned Readout Tokens for Extracting Large Language Model Confidence
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.

items.title: Learning Out of Hours: A Narrative Review of Balancing Responsibility, Supervision, and Fatigue in Junior Doctor Training
items.abstract: Out-of-hours work is an integral component of postgraduate medical training and exposes junior doctors to clinical responsibility, uncertainty, competing demands, and acute deterioration in circumstances that may differ substantially from routine daytime practice. These conditions can provide valuable opportunities for experiential learning, but they can also reduce educational value when responsibility is accompanied by inadequate supervision, excessive workload or fatigue. This narrative review examines out-of-hours work as a learning environment for junior doctors, integrating literature on workplace learning, autonomy and supervision, prioritisation and decision-making, deterioration and escalation, handover and teamwork, sleep disruption and fatigue, and educational interventions designed to prepare trainees for out-of-hours practice. The literature suggests that the educational value of out-of-hours work arises not from independence alone, but from meaningful clinical responsibility within an appropriately supported environment. Responsibility can provide opportunities for autonomous initial assessment, prioritisation, and decision-making under uncertainty, while the recognition of personal limits and appropriate escalation are themselves components of developing clinical judgement. Simulation and structured preparation may help trainees rehearse these demands before substantial clinical responsibility is assumed, while feedback, reflection, and review of subsequent patient outcomes can help convert clinical exposure into learning. However, excessive workload, inadequate supervision, and fatigue may impair both the opportunity and the capacity to learn. Out-of-hours training should therefore aim to preserve authentic responsibility while ensuring that autonomy is graded to capability, senior support remains accessible, workload is manageable, and opportunities for feedback and recovery are maintained. We propose that effective out-of-hours learning occurs within a zone of meaningful responsibility in which trainees are sufficiently challenged to develop clinical judgement without becoming unsupported or physiologically unsustainable. Designing this environment requires attention not only to individual preparedness but also to supervision, staffing, workload, handover, feedback, and rota design.

items.title: Leveraging AI for Higher Education Human Resources:A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Human Resource Development (HRD) policies for academic staff in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) is often constrained by the misalignment between computational capabilities and institutional governance. While HEIs generate substantial datasets through the Tri Dharma (the three pillars of higher education: teaching, research, and community service), this data remains underutilized for proactive policy-making. To map the state-of-the-art and identify existing research gaps, this study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and bibliometric analysis of 400 unique peer-reviewed documents, obtained from an initial 485 records retrieved from Scopus (n = 260) and Web of Science (n = 225) after removing 85 duplicates, covering the seven-year period from 2018 to 2024. Visual analysis using VOSviewer reveals a distinct semantic-policy discrepancy, showing that semantic technologies and predictive AI models are researched as isolated technical domains, seldom integrated into comprehensive institutional governance. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development. The proposed framework integrates machine learning classifiers (Naïve Bayes, K-Means, and Apriori association) with a semantic Knowledge Graph layer to transform descriptive academic metrics into explainable, policy-conforming recommendations. Preliminary expert consultation with LLDIKTI Region II highlights the conceptual viability of the Framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development in mitigating administrative bottlenecks, supporting objective career path design, and minimizing human subjectivity in lecturer performance evaluations.

items.title: LLM agents in online communities draw fewer replies and more disagreement when labeled as AI
items.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) accounts now post, reply, and vote alongside people in online communities. Visible identity labels may act as cultural markers that set these accounts apart from human participants. In a field experiment on YSocial, a Reddit-like platform, 36 students at a Serbian university discussed globally circulated popular culture in English alongside 72 AI accounts with persistent personas and relationship-specific memories over 21 experiment days. AI accounts were labeled in one community and unlabeled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, the estimated probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher under hidden labels, given the same eligible earlier thread contributions (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In browser telemetry, the disadvantage of AI-authored posts in direct thread entry from the feed was 4.4 percentage points smaller under hidden labels (95% credible interval 0.8–8.1). In both communities, participants were more likely to answer an AI account that had just replied to them. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4), mainly criticism of content; the corresponding gap in downvotes from other participants was also larger there, and nearly all references to AI identity occurred there. Toxicity differences were uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less selection and more criticism of AI contributions.

items.title: Lo transido: límite ontológico de la inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: Thinking of the anguished as the ontological limit of artificial intelligence (AI) implies shifting the discussion from techniques to the mode of being. In the cybernetic discourse on AI, the logic of progressive overcoming predominates: more data, more speed, more simulation capacity. However, this logic presupposes that the difference between human and AI is quantitative, when in reality it is ontological. The anguished names precisely that which cannot be increased or optimized, because it is a condition of existence and entails physical and moral pain, as well as a dejection that traverses the human being. The anguished in the human is traversed by the world and the cyberworld as a planetary hybrid. It involves registering stimuli and processing information and being affected in one own being by what happens. Pain is a bodily fact and an experience that wounds, that marks, that leaves a trace on subjects, who are biological, psychological, and social entities; Time is an ordered sequence of moments and an experience of finitude, of waiting, of loss, and of anticipating death. Humanity knows this planetary hybrid and is exposed, compromised, and vulnerable to it. AI, on the other hand, can model pain, recognize its signs, and describe it with increasing precision, but it cannot suffer it. It can calculate time, anticipate future scenarios, and optimize decisions, but it does not experience time as finitude or angst.

items.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.

items.title: Local Faces of Global Employment Practices: Media Discourses on Uberization of Labor and Institutional Adaptation
items.abstract: Uberization has become a paradigmatic case of how platform-mediated work arrangements disrupt labour markets and existing institutional structures, yet we know little about the discursive processes through which such models are reworked within divergent capitalist systems. This article investigates how Uber’s employment model is received, contested and reshaped in the United Kingdom, Germany and Mexico. Linking translation theory and Varieties of Capitalism within a discursive legitimation perspective, we examine how global platform employment practices are received, contested, and evaluated across national institutional contexts. Empirically, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of 3,771 newspaper articles (2012–2023) from the three countries, combining sentiment classification with thematic analysis. We identify discursive waves of (de)legitimation around Uber’s labour practices in distinct institutional constellations. The analysis reveals three trajectories: reactive accommodation under competitive and consumer pressures in the United Kingdom as a liberal market economy; proactive regulatory resistance rooted in labour institutions in Germany as a coordinated market economy; and delayed but intense contestation in Mexico as an emerging market economy characterized by hybrid, fragmented and highly informal arrangements. The study extends the discursive legitimation perspective by linking institutional theory and industrial relations theory to show how institutionally conditioned media discourses shape the (de)legitimation of global employment practices, while bringing emerging markets and informality more centrally into Varieties of Capitalism debates.

items.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
items.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.

items.title: Looks Fine to Me: Understanding Oversight in Agentic Interactions
items.abstract: Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

items.title: Los riesgos de la IA dialógica en la educación superior: afectaciones cognitivas y en la capacidad de lecto-escritura
items.abstract: Dialogic Artificial Intelligence (DAI) or communicative AI within Large Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly expanding across higher education and academic workflows in both teaching and research. The adoption of DAI is being driven by the pressure to enhance productivity and automate academic practices. This paper discusses the primary risks that the intensive use of DAI poses to human cognitive capacities, information biases, and the erosion of literacy, critical thinking, argumentation, and academic discourse skills. Furthermore, it analyzes emerging forms of plagiarism and misconduct facilitated by DAI while reflecting on the concept of individual authorship, which has become obsolete, giving way to human-AI co-authorship. As an immersive technology that impacts human agency and autonomy, DAI could irreversibly transform cognition, literacy, the sense of authorship, and collaborative frameworks in research, teaching, and scholarly production. Finally, it concludes with a set of criteria and recommendations to guide university regulatory policies on DAI, moving beyond prohibitions, punitive measures, or ineffective appeals to individual ethics in the use of LLMs.

items.title: Mammography datasets and artificial intelligence for breast cancer detection: challenges, bias, and future directions
items.abstract: Background Breast cancer is still one of the main causes of death in women from cancer worldwide, and early detection is crucial. Mammography is the primary imaging modality for breast cancer screening and recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly enhanced automated breast cancer detection. This review takes a data-centered approach, examining key characteristics of public datasets, the contributions of mammography data to AI for breast cancer detection, and the implications for clinical generalizability. This review, however, takes a data-centered approach, critically analyzing characteristics of publicly available mammography datasets, and the role of mammography data to the development, performance and clinical generalization of AI models for the detection of breast cancer. The datasets are compared on the following aspects: dataset size, quality of the annotations, imaging modality, clinical metadata, dataset accessibility and demographic diversity. Analysis reveals that the quality, diversity and representativeness of the data used are critical for the performance and generalizability of AI models, ranging from the traditional machine learning era to the current era of deep learning, transformer-based systems, multimodal learning, explainable AI and privacy-preserving learning. Conclusion The results show that, apart from the development of AI model architectures, it is a necessity to have standardized, diverse and clinically representative datasets to make further progress in AI-assisted mammography. The review emphasizes the importance of establishing a comprehensive benchmark dataset for mammography that is large and diverse to enhance reproducibility, to fairly evaluate models, and to develop strong, clinically viable AI systems for breast cancer detection.

items.title: Manifold-Informed Neural Networks for Low-Label ECG Electrolyte Inference
items.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise on the residual of a known differential operator. Many high-stakes inference problems admit no such operator: clinical signals, behavioral measurements, materials properties. We introduce the Manifold-Informed Neural Network (MINN), a PINN-parallel paradigm that replaces the physics operator residual with a manifold operator residual: a discrete Poisson equation $\mathbf{L}_G \mathbf{H} = s_ϕ(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m})$ on a $k$-nearest-neighbor graph in the learned latent space, with a learned, task-aware source. The construction is a structural parallel to PINNs (squared operator residual plus label data, in place of operator residual plus boundary data); the $s{=}0$ limit recovers the homogeneous Laplace equation $\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{0}$ (classical manifold regularization solves the same equation but minimizes the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H})$, a different penalty form). The source $s_ϕ$ takes input features and auxiliary metadata directly, breaking the homogeneous smoothness prior that limits classical Laplacian penalties; gated Feature-wise Linear Modulation separately fuses metadata into the prediction branch. We evaluate MINN on three-class classification of potassium, calcium, and magnesium from 12-lead ECGs in MIMIC-IV-ECG, against twelve baselines spanning supervised and tabular methods, ECG foundation models, and manifold/graph approaches. MINN attains the highest K$^+$ Macro-F1 of 0.61 (best baseline 0.55), with consistent gains on Ca$^{2+}$ and Mg$^{2+}$ and a 31% relative improvement at 1% labeled data. Six targeted ablations show that the inhomogeneous Poisson formulation, not graph smoothing alone, drives the gain.

items.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.abstract: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

items.title: Measuring the spread of trust and distrust through influence in human-autonomy teams
items.abstract: Trust in human-autonomy teams is dynamic and shaped by ongoing interaction, yet most measures rely on retrospective self-report, limiting detection of how trust and distrust propagate in real time. This study introduces and validates influence-an interaction-based metric computed as the average mutual information between joint and team-state time series-to track the spread of trust and distrust. Forty-five participants completed five simulated Remotely Piloted Aircraft System missions in three-member teams, with trust manipulated through communicative and behavioural spreading across congruent, mismatched, and human-versus-agent conditions. Influence predicted subjective team trust and objective performance during active spreading but not in a no-spreading control and showed strong reliability and construct validity. As validation checks, influence recovered known effects: credibility violations damaged trust most, and human sources outweighed agents. Critically, the influence-trust relationship reversed direction across contexts, revealing a context-dependent mechanism. Influence thus offers a real-time, unobtrusive measure linking interaction structure to team outcomes.

items.abstract: Translating preclinical findings into safe and effective pharmacotherapy for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remains a major challenge in pediatric neuropsychopharmacology.This review critically examines why some mechanism-based therapies translate successfully from animal models to clinical practice, whereas others fail despite promising preclinical evidence.Among available models, the spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) exhibits strong construct validity and domain-specific predictive validity for conserved catecholaminergic mechanisms relevant to ADHD.Across species, successful therapies generally preserve mechanistic continuity by enhancing prefrontal catecholamine signaling through dopamine transporter inhibition, norepinephrine transporter blockade, or 2A-adrenergic receptor stimulation.Accordingly, stimulants, atomoxetine, guanfacine, and viloxazine extended-release show substantial translational and clinical success.Pediatric trials support this hierarchy, with clinician-rated standardized mean differences versus placebo of approximately 1.02 for amphetamines, 0.78 for methylphenidate, and 0.56 for atomoxetine at around 12 weeks.In contrast, nicotinic and histaminergic agents and certain dopaminergic antagonist strategies have translated poorly because of inadequate target engagement, developmental pharmacokinetic differences, and pediatric safety concerns.Importantly, SHR predictive validity is domain-specific rather than syndrome-wide, as methylphenidate more consistently improves attention and impulsivity than locomotor hyperactivity.Precision medicine, pharmacogenomics, biomarker-guided target engagement, and artificial intelligence-assisted approaches may improve future drug development.Overall, current evidence supports mechanistic continuity, rather than broad behavioral similarity, as a useful framework for translating preclinical findings into effective pediatric ADHD therapies, although prospective evaluation and refinement of this framework remain necessary.

items.title: Media Intelligence Platform: Multimodal Detection of Synthetic and Manipulated Content
items.abstract: The rapid progress of generative artificial intelligence has led to a significant increase in manipulated multimedia content, including synthetic faces, forged videos, AI-generated images, fake audio, and locally edited images. Existing detection approaches are typically designed for a single manipulation type, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios involving heterogeneous media sources. In this work, we present the Media Intelligence Platform (MIP), a unified web-based framework for multimodal media forensics integrating specialized modules for fake video detection, face morphing detection, AI-generated image detection, audio deepfake detection, localized image manipulation detection, and text analysis. Its modular architecture enables flexible integration of heterogeneous models and supports future extensions for emerging manipulation techniques. Experimental results on representative benchmark datasets demonstrate reliable detection performance across multiple media modalities while providing a practical and user-friendly interface for forensic investigations. The platform highlights the potential of unified multimodal systems for comprehensive deepfake detection in real-world environments, and is accompanied by a public demonstrator released with this workshop submission to support reproducibility and community evaluation.

items.title: Methodological, Data-Related, and Governance Challenges
items.abstract: This chapter critically examines the methodological, data-related, and governance challenges that constrain the effective and responsible implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science. It positions these limitations as a necessary counterbalance to prevailing technological optimism and situates them within both practical modelling workflows and broader epistemological considerations. Building on previous chapters, the analysis emphasizes the importance of validation, robustness testing, and sensitivity analysis as essential components of reliable AI systems. The chapter identifies key barriers to implementation, including economic constraints, limited access to qualified personnel, and institutional resistance-driven by cultural skepticism toward algorithmic decision-making. It further explores the tension between underutilization and overreliance on AI, highlighting risks associated with automation bias and the erosion of human expertise. From a governance perspective, the chapter examines the need for standardization, certification, and auditability, referencing frameworks such as the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and NIST guidelines. It also addresses issues of accessibility and equity, advocating for the democratization of AI technologies through open-access tools and federated learning approaches. The chapter concludes by emphasizing sustainability, stakeholder trust, and the integration of ethical, educational, and regulatory mechanisms as prerequisites for long-term AI adoption in Sports Science.

items.title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records
items.abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.

items.title: Modeling Environments and Their Relevance for Sports Science
items.abstract: This chapter examines the role of modelling environments in Artificial Intelligence workflows within Sports Science, emphasizing that analytical outcomes are shaped not only by algorithms and data but also by the software platforms used for implementation. It conceptualizes modelling environments as cognitive interfaces that mediate between domain expertise and computational reasoning, influencing data preparation, model development, interpretation, and communication of results. The chapter introduces four widely used environments—JASP, SPSS, MATLAB, and R/RStudio—and evaluates their relevance for different stages of AI modelling. Each platform is analyzed in terms of usability, transparency, extensibility, and alignment with the competencies of Sport Science practitioners. Particular attention is given to their strengths and limitations in handling statistical modeling, Machine Learning, Time-Series Analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence. In addition, the chapter highlights the importance of reproducibility through the use of external repositories and LLM-assisted programming workflows. It argues for a complementary, workflow-oriented approach in which multiple environments are combined to address complex analytical tasks. By situating modelling environments within a broader methodological framework, the chapter provides a principled foundation for selecting appropriate tools and supports the development of transparent, reproducible, and data-driven practices in sports analytics and performance modeling.

items.title: Molecular genetic features and prevalence of tetracycline resistance genes in Salmonella enterica
items.abstract: Objective. To assess prevalence of genetic determinants of tetracycline resistance (tetA, tetB, tetC) in Salmonella in the Krasnoyarsk Territory and to identify the most epidemiologically significant tet genes. Materials and Methods. The study included Salmonella cultures isolated in the Krasnoyarsk Territory during the diagnosis of acute intestinal infections, occupational health examinations, and sanitary-epidemiological investigations. Identification was based on morphological and staining characteristics, as well as cultural, biochemical, antigenic properties and phage lysis. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined using the disk diffusion method. The presence of tetA, tetB, and tetC genes was determined by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), followed by electrophoretic detection of amplification products in agarose gel. Results. A total of 67 strains classified as resistant or moderately sensitive to tetracycline based on phenotypic testing were examined. Resistance determinants were detected in 76,1 ± 6,9% of isolates. The prevalence of the tetA gene was 70,1 ± 5,2%, tetB – 7,8 ± 3,4%, and tetC – 8,3 ± 4,0%. Simultaneous presence of tetA and tetB was found in 3,1 ± 5,0% of isolates; tetA and tetC – in 6,3 ± 7,4%. All strains carrying two loci exhibited phenotypic resistance. Conclusions. The tetA gene was the main determinant of tetracycline resistance in Salmonella, detected in 70,2 ± 5,6% of isolates. The tetB and tetC genes were significantly less common — 7,8 ± 3,4% and 8,3 ± 4,0%, respectively. Given that tetA, tetB, and tetC are associated with mobile genetic elements, their horizontal transfer to other microorganisms is highly likely and of epidemiological concern.

items.title: Motivation as the Engine of ESL Success: Exploring Economic, Social, and Educational Determinants of Language Learning
items.abstract: Motivation represents one of the most influential factors affecting success in learning English as a second language (ESL). Although English proficiency is increasingly associated with academic achievement, professional advancement, and global mobility, students' willingness to engage in language learning is shaped by a complex interaction of economic, psychological, pedagogical, and sociocultural influences. Guided by Self-Determination Theory and the L2 Motivational Self System, this paper examines the major factors affecting student motivation in ESL learning. The discussion is organised around four interconnected dimensions: economic and instrumental motivations, academic self-efficacy and personal growth, pedagogical environments and motivational engagement, and cultural curiosity and media exposure. The analysis suggests that students are strongly motivated by career aspirations, financial stability, academic achievement, and communicative competence. At the same time, self-confidence, reduced communication anxiety, supportive learning environments, and exposure to authentic English-language media contribute significantly to sustained motivation. The paper further argues that teacher attitudes, innovative pedagogical practices, and opportunities for meaningful communication play a central role in transforming external motivation into internal commitment to language learning. Motivation is therefore conceptualised as a dynamic process shaped by personal aspirations and environmental influences rather than a fixed individual characteristic. Future research should investigate the role of artificial intelligence-assisted learning, digital motivation, multilingual identity, and long-term motivational development among ESL learners.

items.title: Multi-agent LLMs on the Cloud-Edge-IoT Continuum: A Systematic Mapping Study on Architectures, Deployment, and Evaluation
items.abstract: LLM applications are increasingly built as systems of cooperating components rather than as single prompt-response pipelines. IoT applications add constraints of their own, because sensing, reasoning, control, and actuation are spread across devices, edge nodes, and cloud services to meet latency, privacy, and bandwidth requirements. How multi-agent LLM systems are organized and deployed across this cloud-edge-IoT continuum has not been mapped systematically. We therefore conducted a systematic mapping study. From 831 records retrieved up to March 2026, we selected 45 primary studies and classified each one by architecture family, deployment pattern, application domain, and evaluation practice. We also recorded how each system was evaluated and whether its code or data are public. Five architecture families recur in the corpus. Specialized agent teams run next to sensors, planners delegate subtasks to workers, and small local models cooperate with large cloud models. A fourth group federates model adaptation across devices, and a large fifth group builds the supporting infrastructure for offloading, communication, memory, and serving. Deployment relies on six recurring patterns, ranging from local-only execution to control loops gated by policy checks or human approval. Twenty-four of the 45 studies target IoT, industrial, smart-home, healthcare, vehicular, or robotics settings, and 29 evaluate on physical hardware, where open models below 8B parameters dominate. Based on the mapping, we list the reporting items needed to make future evaluations comparable, give deployment guidance for common IoT constraints, and identify open problems.

items.title: Multi-objective deep deterministic policy gradient for cobot trajectory planning in automotive spot welding
items.abstract: Introduction Autonomous trajectory planning is a fundamental challenge in collaborative robotic spot welding because positioning accuracy, motion smoothness, operational safety, energy use, and production efficiency must be optimized simultaneously under industrial constraints. Methods This paper presents a Pareto-Guided Multi-Objective Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (PMO-DDPG) framework for autonomous cobot trajectory planning in automotive spot welding. The framework combines a deterministic actor with four objective-specific critics for accuracy, smoothness, safety, and productivity, together with phase-dependent preferences for the approach, alignment, welding, and retraction stages. The principal novelty is a two-level multi-objective design that preserves six normalized physical reward components, maps them to four specialized critics for phase-dependent actor updates, and uses a non-dominated policy archive for Pareto-guided selection while retaining actor-only online inference. Simulation and industrial experiments assessed convergence, trajectory quality, collision avoidance, energy consumption, cycle time, success rate, and latency. Results Relative to the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) baseline, PMO-DDPG reduced trajectory error by 66.4%, collision rate by 82.1%, energy consumption by 15.5%, cycle time by 22.0%, and inference latency by 22.7%, while increasing the success rate by 7.5 percentage points. The proposed method achieved 1.08 mm trajectory error, a 1.2% collision rate, 3.65 kJ energy consumption, a 3.87 s cycle time, a 94.6% success rate, and 21.5 ms inference time. Pareto-front analysis produced non-dominated operating points for different manufacturing priorities, and 100 industrial trials confirmed sub-millimeter positioning and repeatable vision-guided welding. Discussion Within the evaluated simulation and industrial test settings, and without a formal significance test, these descriptive results indicate that PMO-DDPG is a promising accurate, safe, and efficient trajectory-planning approach.

items.title: Multifunctional Alginate–TiO2/SiO2 Hydrogel–Ceramic Composites for Photocatalytic Soil Remediation and Impedance-Based Diagnostics: A Critical Review and Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Soil contamination by persistent organic pollutants is a major environmental challenge, whereas conventional remediation approaches often lack effective means for continuous, in situ monitoring of treatment progress. Recent advances in multifunctional materials provide a basis for integrating pollutant degradation with non-destructive environmental monitoring. This review critically examines alginate–TiO2/SiO2 hydrogel–ceramic composites as a potential platform for integrating photocatalytic soil remediation with impedance-based monitoring. TiO2 exhibits photocatalytic activity and promotes the generation of reactive oxygen species; SiO2 contributes to adsorption, dispersion, porosity, and structural stability; while sodium alginate provides a hydrated, biodegradable matrix for particle immobilization, water retention, and mass-transport control. Particular attention is given to electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) as a non-destructive method for monitoring time-dependent physicochemical changes in soil–composite systems. This review evaluates suitable composite architectures, electrode configurations, calibration strategies, control experiments, and approaches for interpreting complex impedance responses. The potential application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning is also considered, with emphasis on data quality, independent validation, and the limitations of models trained on heterogeneous environmental datasets. Because impedance responses are inherently indirect and non-specific, chemical analysis remains essential for confirming pollutant transformation and identifying transformation products. Standardized ecotoxicological assays, particularly reproduction testing with the springtail Folsomia candida, are considered as an independent biological line of evidence for determining whether physicochemical improvements are accompanied by reduced residual toxicity. Key challenges include heterogeneous soil properties, limited light penetration, mass-transfer limitations, catalyst and hydrogel stability, sensor calibration, matrix effects, and model accuracy. The review proposes an evidence-based framework linking material design, photocatalytic treatment, EIS monitoring, chemical verification, and ecotoxicological assessment. However, the complete integrated platform has not yet been experimentally validated, and its performance in real contaminated soils remains to be established.

items.title: Multimodal artificial intelligence for vascular aging: toward proactive detection and management
items.abstract: Vascular aging is a fundamental driver of cardiovascular diseases (CVD), yet identifying individuals undergoing accelerated vascular aging - and therefore at elevated cardiovascular risk - remains a significant clinical challenge. The traditional “one-size-fits-all” health risk assessments are often insensitive to early, subclinical vascular changes. The recent explosion of medical big data, coupled with the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), offer a transformative opportunity to shift vascular aging management from reactive detection toward proactive, predictive protection. This review systematically explores the integration of multimodal artificial intelligence (MMAI) and large-scale foundation models in the identification, stratification, and personalized management of vascular aging. We first delineate the multidimensional data ecosystem of vascular aging, including electronic health records (EHRs), imaging, omics, and continuous physiological signals from wearables, and analyze how deep learning architectures enable the detection of vascular aging by capturing subclinical structural and functional alterations. We then focus on the emerging role of MFMs, which transcend task-specific AI by integrating heterogeneous data types to provide holistic phenomapping. Furthermore, we discuss the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) in clinical workflows, enhancing patient adherence through natural language interaction, and accelerating research through knowledge synthesis. Despite the potential of foundation models, their clinical translation faces technical and institutional barriers. We analyze four systemic challenges: algorithmic fairness, regulatory uncertainty, explainable AI (XAI) and the lack of real-world validation. We propose a strategic roadmap aligned with international frameworks that progresses from standardized performance reporting for elderly subgroups in the near term to cost-effective, individualized interventions that intercept the health-to-disease transition in the long term. The convergence of big data and foundation models represents a shift from reactive cardiovascular care to proactive, precision-based longevity management, positioning early, AI-enabled identification of high-risk vascular aging phenotypes as a primary target for the next generation of preventive medicine.

items.title: Multimodal Large-Model-Driven Method for Urban 3D Green-Space Calculation and Low-Carbon Green-Space Management
items.abstract: Against the background of global carbon neutrality goals and urban ecological transformation, traditional two-dimensional green-space indicators cannot fully reflect spatial–ecological benefits, and conventional 3D green-space calculation and landscape maintenance methods suffer from low accuracy and low efficiency. This paper proposes a theoretical technical framework combining multimodal remote sensing data, LiDAR point clouds and domain large language models for urban green-space scenarios. Firstly, a multimodal feature fusion strategy is constructed to adapt to complex urban environments, and a hierarchical calculation workflow for individual trees and regional 3D green-space is designed. Secondly, a full-life-cycle carbon accounting system for landscape engineering is established, which clarifies the accounting boundaries and quantitative methods of carbon sources and carbon sinks. Thirdly, a human–computer collaborative decision framework is proposed to realise intelligent recommendations for low-carbon maintenance schemes. This study focuses on theoretical framework construction and method exploration, and verifies the technical feasibility through simulation analysis. Different from existing independent research on green-space calculation or carbon accounting, this work integrates the two tasks and innovates a multimodal model application mode for landscape industry. This study focuses on theoretical framework construction and methodological exploration; feasibility assessment is only carried out via simulation deduction, rather than real-world field validation.

items.title: Multimodal Learning for Time Series Forecasting: Architectures, Challenges, and New Directions
items.abstract: Time series forecasting increasingly exploits information that is not itself a numerical series, such as news text, imagery, contextual metadata, and relational structure among series. The term "multimodal" is nonetheless used without an operational definition, so that genuinely cross-modal models are pooled with multivariate and multi-view models that raise different problems. This paper proposes an operational criterion, together with a four-question procedure, that separates multimodal forecasting from multivariate, multi-view, and cross-modal model-reuse settings. On this basis it develops a five-axis taxonomy covering modality type, temporal alignment granularity, fusion mechanism, model family, and output form with uncertainty representation, and presents a structured synthesis of 33 published studies across eight application domains. Applying the criterion consistently shows that only 14 studies fully satisfy the definition. Notably, five large-language-model-based forecasters presented as series–text alignment methods use only text generated from the input series itself, which cannot add information about the future. Combined with published ablation evidence, this indicates that the benefit of an auxiliary modality is conditional rather than universal, and that evaluation practice, rather than architecture, is the binding constraint of the field. Generalisation under a shifting context–target relationship — the very condition auxiliary context is expected to address — remains essentially untested. The paper analyses seven groups of open challenges and proposes five research directions, notably multimodal self-supervised learning and offline semantic feature extraction with large language models, together with an eight-item minimum evaluation protocol intended to make the contribution of an auxiliary modality verifiable.

items.title: MuPACE: Learning to Pace Muon for LoRA Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: Learning rate schedules are typically fixed before training begins, yet when fine-tuning large language models with low-rank adapters (LoRA), the appropriate scale varies substantially with the model, task, and adapter configuration. Practitioners re-tune a schedule for every new problem, yet a tuned schedule still cannot react to the training dynamics it encounters. We instead amortize learning rate selection across LoRA fine-tuning problems. We leave the base optimizer, Muon, untouched, so that its normalized update fixes the direction, and meta-learn only the global step size. Our method MuPACE is a small recurrent policy, meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning runs, that conditions on the observed trajectory and emits bounded adjustments to an interpretable analytic schedule. On 64 fine-tuning problems, MuPACE outperforms standard fixed schedules at a strong shared default on 64-78% of problems and is on par with the same schedules with per-task tuned peaks. Meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE transfers one-shot to unseen tasks on models as deep as 64 layers, such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, where a single run remains competitive with swept schedules.

items.title: Musical Giftedness in Human-AI Creation: Interpreting Evidence Beyond the Finished Product
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence complicates a central problem in identifying musical giftedness: deciding which features of an outcome can reasonably be attributed to the student who presents it. A piece may display coherent formal design, an elaborate harmonic plan, idiomatic instrumentation, or convincing timbral balance even when those decisions were neither made nor understood by the learner. This conceptual article examines how music co-created with AI can be interpreted when the finished product no longer reveals the student’s contribution on its own. Drawing on research on musical talent development, AI-assisted creation, and assessment validity, it considers three sources of information: compositional problem framing, analytical listening and revision, and the traceability of musical decisions. Transfer across tasks provides a further check. These sources are not diagnostic criteria. They are intended to support more cautious interpretations of musical evidence in AI-mediated creative work and to complement broader developmental evidence used in identification processes.

items.title: Nanobiosensors at the Frontier: A Comprehensive Review on the Design, Digital Integration, and Clinical Applications for Next‐Generation Precision Diagnostics
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Recent progress in nanotechnology and biosensing is driving the development of advanced diagnostic tools for precision medicine. This review provides a systematic summary and critical analysis of intelligent nanobiosensors, which integrate engineered nanomaterials with biological recognition components and advanced signal‐transduction mechanisms. Key design paradigms, classification frameworks, and the role of diverse nanomaterials (e.g., metallic, carbon‐based, magnetic, and hybrid structures) are discussed in detail. Furthermore, major transduction technologies, including electrochemical, optical, mechanical, thermal, and magnetic platforms, together with clinical translation pathways and integration with artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing, and mobile health technologies, are comprehensively reviewed. Particular emphasis is placed on clinical applications in infectious, oncological, cardiovascular, and neurological diseases, as well as therapeutic monitoring. Key challenges, including scalability, data security, and regulatory barriers, are also critically discussed. Finally, emerging trends such as federated learning, the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), and personalized digital diagnostics are highlighted, providing perspectives on future directions in intelligent biosensing and precision healthcare.

items.title: Natural-language prompting builds and operates an open-source software workflow for virtual drug-discovery
items.abstract: Virtual docking and free-energy calculations can accelerate drug discovery, but practical use requires structural chemistry expertise, complex parameter selection and software integration. Here we show that iterative dialogue with an artificial intelligence (AI) coding assistant, OpenAI Codex, can guide a non-specialist scientist to build and operate a scripted, auditable computational workflow without direct coding. The assistant provided structural chemistry guidance and assembled an integrated pipeline for structure retrieval and preparation, binding-site definition, ligand preparation, virtual docking, interaction analysis, molecular dynamics (MD) and alchemical relative binding free-energy calculations. It also built a script generator for launching, monitoring and interpreting workflow runs. We tested the workflow on public cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) benchmarks. After primary docking and multi-seed hit refinement, the active-ligand fraction increased from 1.73% in the input library to 80% in the ten-candidate handoff set (46.4-fold over input); a short MD stage acted as a structural quality-control gate on the leading candidates. Docking and hit refinement also generalized to human immunodeficiency virus reverse transcriptase and kinesin family member 11 benchmarks. In a CDK2 free-energy benchmark, the workflow achieved root-mean-square error = 0.66 kcal/mol and Pearson r = 0.90. Prompt-guided AI can orchestrate computational drug-discovery workflows for non-specialists while the underlying calculations remain the work of established external software and every run remains auditable.

items.title: Navigating the Recursive Loop: A Systems Dynamics Perspective on Conversational AI, Socio-Technical Feedback, and Human Psychological Resilience
items.abstract: Severe chronic distress and acute emotional episodes present persistent challenges to human relatedness, competence, and autonomy. While traditional clinical psychotherapy establishes the benchmark for evidence-based care, its episodic delivery leaves structural temporal gaps—such as the nocturnal 2:00 AM crisis loop—unsupported. This paper examines the role of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) as an immediate, continuous cognitive scaffold through the lens of Systems Dynamics and Socio-Technical Systems (STS) Theory. By modeling conversational AI interactions through reinforcing and balancing feedback loops, we analyze how automated Socratic inquiry can either accelerate psychological resilience or entrench maladaptive sycophancy. Ultimately, we argue against technological determinism, advocating for joint optimization where technical infrastructure, human agency, and governance frameworks co-evolve.

items.abstract: Kids with autism, ADHD, or dyslexia hit roadblocks in regular schools their brains just work differently when it comes to focusing, thinking, or picking up new stuff at their own pace. You'll get helpers to stay on track, clean layouts that won't stress you out, game-like challenges to make it fun, and choices for seeing, hearing, or doing activities. All this ramps up what sticks in your head without overwhelming you, helps you learn on your own, and ditches that nagging school worry. Parents and teachers see updates as you go. Bottom line, NeuroLearn smooths out the bumps, making education fair for everyone—no matter how your mind ticks. items.title: Non-Recognition of Online Doctoral Programs in India in the Era of AI, Education 4.0, and Education 5.0: Challenges for Working Professionals
items.abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and digitally mediated learning has intensified debate about flexibility, access, and quality assurance in higher education. This study examines stakeholder perceptions of the non-recognition of fully online doctoral education in India, focusing on career barriers, psychological burnout, acceptance of Education 4.0, institutional resistance, and support for policy reform. Using a cross-sectional questionnaire dataset of 832 respondents, the study applies descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), group comparisons, and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. The findings indicate comparatively high mean scores for perceived career barriers and Education 4.0 acceptance. Group comparisons did not identify statistically significant differences across the categories examined. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F(7, 824) = 64.28, p < 0.001; R² = 0.353; adjusted R² = 0.348). Institutional resistance was positively associated with policy-reform support, whereas career barriers showed a smaller negative association. Education 4.0 acceptance also showed a positive association with reform support. These findings represent statistical relationships within the sample and do not establish causal effects. The study contributes to discussions on Indian higher-education policy by outlining considerations for a quality-assured framework that addresses research supervision, assessment, academic integrity, institutional accountability, and equitable access to doctoral education.

items.title: NousDB - A Fast Query Engine for Semantic Analytics
items.abstract: Semantic data analytics systems integrate AI-powered operators into query pipelines, enabling declarative queries over structured and unstructured data. However, existing systems rely on per-tuple model invocations, ad hoc operator designs, and lack principled cost models, resulting in poor scalability and limited optimization. We present NousDB, a high-performance semantic analytics engine built on Apache DataFusion[22]. Through NousDB we propose an extended relational algebra with three semantic operators and formal algebraic properties that enable principled query rewriting and cross-operator optimization. We further propose a token-based cost model using equi-depth token histograms to optimize batch sizing under context-window constraints and provide statistical guarantees for safe batching. Experiments show that NousDB achieves up to x86 speedups with both local and enterprise LLMs, while leading competitors in token efficiency and accuracy.
